Five habits that made my sleep steadier

For most of last year I slept badly, and I assumed the problem was my mattress, my schedule or some fault in me that no amount of tinkering would fix. It turned out to be mostly a handful of small habits.

The first change was the simplest: I stopped drinking coffee after noon. It felt like a trivial rule, but within a week I was falling asleep faster and waking less often during the night.

The second was a fixed wake-up time, including at weekends. Sleeping in felt like a reward, yet it quietly pushed my body clock later and made Monday mornings far harder than they needed to be.

Third, I moved my phone out of the bedroom. A cheap alarm clock replaced it, and the evening scroll that used to stretch past midnight gave way to a few pages of a paperback instead.

Fourth, I started getting outside within an hour of waking. Even ten minutes of daylight seemed to anchor the rest of the day, and I noticed that I felt sleepy at a sensible hour for the first time in years.

Last, I stopped treating a bad night as a disaster. Worrying about sleep turned out to be its own cause of wakefulness, and letting a poor night pass without a fuss made the next one noticeably better.
